title: Near-Optimal Ground-State Preparation without Controlled Hamiltonian Evolutions
authors: Dhrumil Patel, Steven T. Flammia, Raul Garcia-Patron
abstract: Ground-state preparation, energy estimation, and property estimation are fundamental tasks in quantum simulation. Existing ground-state preparation algorithms achieve near-optimal complexity using block encodings or controlled Hamiltonian evolution, raising a natural question: is controlled Hamiltonian evolution necessary, or can the same scaling be attained in the weaker access model that provides access to only uncontrolled Hamiltonian evolution? We resolve this question by giving two algorithms that access the input Hamiltonian $H$ only through queries to $U_H$ and its inverse $U_H^\dagger$, where $\|H\|\leα_H$ and $τ=Θ(1/α_H)$. Given an input state with ground-state weight at least $η$ and a spectral gap of $H$ of at least $γ$, our first algorithm uses fresh copies of the input state and requires $\widetilde O(α_H/(γη))$ queries to $U_H$ and $U_H^\dagger$, while our second algorithm uses coherent access to the input-state preparation unitary and its inverse to improve this complexity to $\widetilde O(α_H/(γ\sqrtη))$. The latter bound matches the known lower bound up to logarithmic factors, showing that algorithms with additional access to controlled Hamiltonian evolution cannot improve the query complexity for ground-state preparation beyond logarithmic factors. Both algorithms are based on a simple mechanism that we call the spectral descent principle, in which the algorithm starts from the input state $|ψ\rangle$ and progressively descends through the energy spectrum, moving closer to the ground state until the desired fidelity is reached. We also extend this framework to ground-state property and energy estimation and give explicit complexity guarantees for both tasks.
summary: This paper develops algorithms for ground-state preparation using only uncontrolled access to the Hamiltonian's time evolution. By employing the Spectral Descent Principle, the authors show that the required query complexity matches established lower bounds, proving that controlled Hamiltonian evolution is not necessary for achieving optimal scaling in this task.
main_problem: Determining if controlled Hamiltonian evolution is necessary for achieving near-optimal query complexity in ground-state preparation (GSP) compared to using only uncontrolled time-evolution access.
main_result: Two algorithms using only uncontrolled evolution achieve complexities matching known lower bounds (up to log factors), demonstrating that controlled evolution offers no asymptotic advantage for GSP.
method: The core technique is the Spectral Descent Principle, which iteratively refines an estimate of the ground state by comparing candidate states to the current best estimate using an Energy Comparator.
model_or_system: The model involves a quantum Hamiltonian H, and the access is restricted to uncontrolled time-evolution unitaries ($U_H = e^{-iH	au}$ and $U_H^\dagger$). The process is analyzed in terms of state overlaps ($\eta$) and spectral gaps ($\gamma$).
key_observables: Ground-state fidelity, energy populations, and the required number of queries to $U_H$ and $U_H^\dagger$.
important_parameters: Hamiltonian norm ($\alpha_H$), spectral gap ($\gamma$), initial state overlap ($\eta$), and the time step ($	au = \Theta(1/\alpha_H)$).
main_assumptions: The algorithms assume promises on the spectral gap ($\gamma$) and the initial state overlap ($\eta$). The second algorithm assumes coherent access to the state preparation unitary ($U_\psi$).
paper_structure: The paper establishes the fundamental problem, presents two algorithms (Spectral Descent and Coherent Spectral Descent) based on the Spectral Descent Principle, and analyzes the complexity bounds achieved using only uncontrolled evolution.
why_interesting: It provides concrete algorithmic results showing that resource limitations (avoiding controlled operations) do not degrade the fundamental scaling of quantum simulation tasks like GSP.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: Figure 3: The t-th descent stage of SD. Each dashed box represents one comparison trial and contains the energy comparator, the measurement-controlled anchor update, and the subsequent discarding of the candidate register. If the measured outcome is q = 0, only the anchor register continues to the next trial, while a new witness qubit is initialized in |0⟩and a fresh candidate state |ψ⟩is prepared in B. If the outcome is q = 1, the candidate is swapped into A and the descent stage terminates. The stage contains at most M comparison trials.

Figure 5: Circuit implementation of one generalized FPAA iterate G(α, β) = −Ssrc(α)Swit(β), up to an irrelevant global phase. The left dashed box implements the witness reflection Swit(β) by applying the single-qubit phase gate P(β) = |0⟩⟨0| + eiβ|1⟩⟨1| to the witness qubit q. The right dashed box implements the source reflection Ssrc(α). The control shown on register B is shorthand for controls on all n qubits of B, and X denotes the Pauli-X gate. Thus, one FPAA iterate uses one application each of Cζ, C† ζ, Uψ, and U† ψ, together with one ancilla qubit.
